title: Relativistic Addition of Velocities
lead: Classically, velocities along one line add like ordinary numbers, $\ku = \kv + \kuprime$, but that cannot be true of light, which every observer measures at $\kc$. Relativistic velocity addition, $\ku = (\kv + \kuprime)/(1 + \kv\kuprime/\kc^{2})$, replaces the classical sum. It returns $\kc$ for a beam of light and keeps every other sum below $\kc$, as a canister shot towards and away from the Earth shows. The same reasoning gives the relativistic Doppler shift: light from a receding source arrives with a longer wavelength, and light from an approaching one with a shorter wavelength.
objectives: Explain when relativistic velocity addition should be used instead of classical addition of velocities.
summary_html:
• With classical velocity addition, velocities add like regular numbers in one-dimensional motion: $\ku = \kv + \kuprime$, where $\kv$ is the velocity between two observers, $\ku$ is the velocity of an object relative to one observer, and $\kuprime$ is the velocity relative to the other observer.
  • Velocities cannot add to be greater than the speed of light. Relativistic velocity addition describes the velocities of an object moving at a relativistic speed: $$\ku = \frac{\kv + \kuprime}{1 + \frac{\kv\kuprime}{\kc^{2}}}$$
  • An observer of electromagnetic radiation sees relativistic Doppler effects if the source of the radiation is moving relative to the observer. The wavelength of the radiation is longer (called a red shift) than that emitted by the source when the source moves away from the observer and shorter (called a blue shift) when the source moves toward the observer. The shifted wavelength is described by the equation $$\klamobs = \klams\sqrt{\frac{1 + \frac{\ku}{\kc}}{1 - \frac{\ku}{\kc}}}$$ $\klamobs$ is the observed wavelength, $\klams$ is the source wavelength, and $\ku$ is the relative velocity of the source to the observer.

figures.original_caption: Classically, velocities add like ordinary numbers in one-dimensional motion. Here the girl throws a snowball forward and then backward from a sled. The velocity of the sled relative to the Earth is v = 1.0 m/s. The velocity of the snowball relative to the sled is u′, while its velocity relative to the Earth is u. Classically, u = v + u′.

According to experiment and the second postulate of relativity, light from the car’s headlights moves away from the car at speed c and towards the observer on the sidewalk at speed c. Classical velocity addition is not valid.

exercises.prompt: Suppose a space probe moves away from the Earth at a speed $0.350c$. It sends a radio wave message back to the Earth at a frequency of 1.50 GHz. At what frequency is the message received on the Earth?

answer.hint: The probe moves away, so $\ku$ is positive, and the received frequency is lower than the one sent.

exercises.prompt: How is the relativistic Doppler effect different from the classical Doppler effect?

answer.solution: The relativistic Doppler effect takes into account the special relativity concept of time dilation and also does not require a medium of propagation to be used as a point of reference (light does not require a medium for propagation).

exercises.prompt: Explain the meaning of the terms “red shift” and “blue shift” as they relate to the relativistic Doppler effect.

answer.solution: A red shift is an increase in the observed wavelength of electromagnetic radiation, which happens when the source moves away from the observer; the wavelength is shifted toward the red, long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum. A blue shift is a decrease in the observed wavelength, which happens when the source moves toward the observer, shifting the wavelength toward the blue end. In the equation $\klamobs = \klams\sqrt{(1 + \ku/\kc)/(1 - \ku/\kc)}$, a positive $\ku$ gives $\klamobs$ larger than $\klams$ and a negative $\ku$ gives it smaller.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the relativistic Doppler effect when relative velocity is zero? Is this the expected result?

answer.solution: With $\ku = 0$, the square root becomes $\sqrt{1/1} = 1$, so $\klamobs = \klams$ and $\kfobs = \kfsrc$. There is no shift at all. This is the expected result, since a Doppler shift comes only from relative motion between the source and the observer.

exercises.prompt: Is the relativistic Doppler effect consistent with the classical Doppler effect in the respect that ${\lambda}_{\text{obs}}$ is larger for motion away?

answer.solution: Yes. For sound, a source moving away from the listener spreads its wave crests farther apart and the observed wavelength is longer. In the relativistic equation, a positive $\ku$ (motion away) makes the numerator $1 + \ku/\kc$ larger than the denominator $1 - \ku/\kc$, so $\klamobs$ is again larger than $\klams$. The two effects agree in direction; they differ in the size of the shift at high speeds and in needing no medium.

exercises.prompt: All galaxies farther away than about $50\times 10^{6}\;\text{ly}$ exhibit a red shift in their emitted light that is proportional to distance, with those farther and farther away having progressively greater red shifts. What does this imply, assuming that the only source of red shift is relative motion? (Hint: At these large distances, it is space itself that is expanding, but the effect on light is the same.)

answer.solution: A red shift means the galaxy is moving away from us, and a greater red shift means a greater speed away. Since the red shift grows in proportion to distance, the more distant a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. This implies that the universe is expanding: every distance between distant galaxies is growing, so that from any galaxy the others appear to move away at speeds proportional to their distances.

exercises.prompt: Suppose a spaceship heading straight towards the Earth at $0.750c$ can shoot a canister at $0.500c$ relative to the ship. (a) What is the velocity of the canister relative to the Earth, if it is shot directly at the Earth? (b) If it is shot directly away from the Earth?

parts.hint: Take towards the Earth as positive, so both $\kv$ and $\kuprime$ are positive.

parts.part: (b) shot directly away from the Earth
parts.hint: Now $\kuprime$ is negative, while the ship still moves towards the Earth.

exercises.prompt: If a spaceship is approaching the Earth at $0.100c$ and a message capsule is sent toward it at $0.100c$ relative to the Earth, what is the speed of the capsule relative to the ship?

answer.hint: In the ship’s frame the Earth approaches at $0.100c$ and the capsule leaves the Earth towards the ship at $0.100c$, so the two velocities add relativistically.

exercises.prompt: If a galaxy moving away from the Earth has a speed of $1000\;\text{km/s}$ and emits $656\;\text{nm}$ light characteristic of hydrogen (the most common element in the universe). (a) What wavelength would we observe on the Earth? (b) What type of electromagnetic radiation is this? (c) Why is the speed of the Earth in its orbit negligible here?

answer.hint: Write the galaxy’s speed as a fraction of $c$ first; it moves away, so $\ku$ is positive.

exercises.prompt: If two spaceships are heading directly towards each other at $0.800c$, at what speed must a canister be shot from the first ship to approach the other at $0.999c$ as seen by the second ship?

answer.hint: In the second ship’s frame, $\ku = 0.999c$ and $\kv = 0.800c$; solve the addition formula for $\kuprime$.

exercises.prompt: When a missile is shot from one spaceship towards another, it leaves the first at $0.950c$ and approaches the other at $0.750c$. What is the relative velocity of the two ships?

answer.hint: Take $\kuprime = 0.950c$ in the first ship’s frame and $\ku = 0.750c$ in the second ship’s frame, then solve the addition formula for $\kv$.

exercises.prompt: Near the center of our galaxy, hydrogen gas is moving directly away from us in its orbit about a black hole. We receive 1900 nm electromagnetic radiation and know that it was 1875 nm when emitted by the hydrogen gas. What is the speed of the gas?

answer.hint: Square the ratio $\klamobs/\klams$ and solve for $\ku/\kc$.

exercises.prompt: Prove that for any relative velocity $v$ between two observers, a beam of light sent from one to the other will approach at speed $c$ (provided that $v$ is less than $c$, of course).

(a) All but the closest galaxies are receding from our own Milky Way Galaxy. If a galaxy $12.0\times 10^{9}\;\text{ly}$ ly away is receding from us at 0.0.900c, at what velocity relative to us must we send an exploratory probe to approach the other galaxy at $0.990c$, as measured from that galaxy? (b) How long will it take the probe to reach the other galaxy as measured from the Earth? You may assume that the velocity of the other galaxy remains constant. (c) How long will it then take for a radio signal to be beamed back? (All of this is possible in principle, but not practical.)

parts.part: (a) the probe’s velocity relative to us
parts.hint: In the galaxy’s frame the probe approaches at $0.990c$, and the galaxy moves away from us at $0.900c$.

parts.part: (b) the travel time measured from the Earth
parts.hint: The probe gains on the galaxy at the difference of their speeds as measured from the Earth.

parts.part: (c) the time for the radio signal to come back
parts.hint: The signal returns at $c$ across the distance the galaxy has reached by then.

answer.solution:
a) $0.99947c$
b) $1.2064\times 10^{11}\;\text{y}$
c) $1.2058\times 10^{11}\;\text{y}$ (all to sufficient digits to show effects)

referents.label: the source, a galaxy or hydrogen gas
the Earth, which receives the waves
